keyVerseText: And when they had called to the king, there came out to them Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, which was over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah the son of Asaph the recorder. scribe: or, secretary
rootMeaning: The name אֶלְיָקִים (ʼElyâqîym) is derived from the Hebrew elements אֵל (ʼêl), meaning 'God' or 'mighty one,' and קוּם (qum), meaning 'to rise' or 'to set up.' Thus, the literal meaning of the name is 'God raises' or 'God sets up.' This root sense emphasizes divine action and authority, suggesting that the individual bearing the name is established or empowered by God’s sovereign will, beyond a mere personal identifier.
usageInScripture: The word אֶלְיָקִים appears twelve times in Scripture, primarily as a proper name referring to four different Israelites, including a prominent servant of King Hezekiah and a son of Josiah. The top translation 'Eliakim' is consistent, occurring eight times, with variations such as 'made Eliakim' indicating God’s appointment or establishment of the person. This consistent use as a personal name tied to divine appointment highlights the theological weight of the name in biblical narrative and history.
theologicalSignificance: The meaning 'God sets up' underscores the biblical truth that positions of authority and leadership are ultimately established by God’s sovereign hand. This reminds believers that human leaders serve under divine authority and that God is the one who raises up and sustains them. In the Christian faith, this reflects the principle that God’s providence governs history and leadership, pointing ultimately to Christ, who is the supreme appointed ruler by God. Recognizing the divine origin of authority calls believers to trust and submit to God’s purposes even when human leadership is imperfect.
keyVerseReflection: In 2 Kings 18:18, Eliakim is introduced as 'the son of Hilkiah, which was over the household,' highlighting his role as a chief official in King Hezekiah’s administration. The use of the name Eliakim here signals that this position of authority is not merely political but carries the weight of divine establishment. The name reminds readers that Eliakim’s stewardship is under God’s sovereign appointment, encouraging trust in God’s governance even amid political challenges.
